stories.headline: Tesla Robotaxi now runs 24/7 in every city it serves
stories.why_read: Round-the-clock service is the clearest sign yet that Tesla trusts its driving software at night and at scale, and it lands the same week San Antonio became the eighth Robotaxi city.
body: Tesla's Robotaxi account posted a two-line update: the service now runs 24/7 in every city where it is available. The post drew thousands of reposts within hours, and fans read it as a signal that FSD performance has cleared another bar, since overnight hours bring darker roads and fewer remote-support staff.

It follows the expansion of unsupervised service to San Antonio, a 274-square-mile area and Tesla's eighth Robotaxi city, which helped push the stock up more than 3.5% toward $395 on November 11. The open questions are when Cybercab additions to the fleet resume and when Robotaxi starts taking freeways, which would open up airport and cross-town trips.

stories.headline: Nvidia is reportedly preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang
stories.why_read: The company that sells the shovels for the whole AI boom may change leaders for the first time in its history. That affects GPU roadmaps, China export politics and every lab's compute plans.
body: The Wall Street Journal reports that Nvidia is preparing to remove Jensen Huang, who co-founded the company and has run it for more than three decades. The story follows Huang's apology to staff over a personal relationship and a board review of an associate's alleged links to Chinese intelligence; some reports say that review found no security breach.

The Hacker News thread passed 1,000 points and 1,400 comments within hours, and X is full of memes and theories, including claims that rivals are fueling the coverage. Watch for an official board statement, an interim CEO name, and how customers like the big labs and hyperscalers react.

stories.headline: On a pre-IPO broker call, Anthropic pitched $1 trillion in yearly revenue by 2028
stories.why_read: The leaked call shows how the company is selling its Nasdaq debut: winner-take-all AI, a giant compute bill, and investor returns as an afterthought.
body: Anthropic's shares are set to start trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT around November 19. A summary of a broker call that leaked online has executives describing AI as a winner-take-all market and aiming for $1 trillion in annual revenue by late 2028, up from a reported $81 billion run rate at the end of October.

The pitch leans on more than $1 trillion of committed infrastructure spending and openly targets hyperscalers, rival labs and chipmakers. Analysts were also told that Anthropic's compute contract with SpaceX won't run past the middle of next year. Reactions range from '$ANT' hype to skeptics pointing out how much the company still depends on the cloud giants it says it will disrupt.

stories.headline: Grok 4.8 finishes pre-training after SpaceXAI rewrote its stack in C and C++
stories.why_read: Dropping JAX and SGLang for hand-written C/C++ is an unusual systems bet for a frontier lab, and a soft rollout to Bot users is expected this week.
body: Elon Musk says Grok 4.8 has finished pre-training after SpaceXAI rebuilt its reinforcement learning and inference stack from scratch in C and C++, replacing JAX and SGLang. The rewrite cost time, but Musk says the model will be very different from Grok 4.7, with evals climbing ahead of a soft launch to Bot users.

SpaceX VP Kiko Dontchev shared an early industrial win: Grok spots debris in aerospace parts with 99.9% accuracy, compared with 94% for human inspectors, and cuts the task from hours to seconds. Musk's summary of the approach: 'Real men manage their own memory.'

stories.headline: Critical remote code execution bug in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module
stories.why_read: Wiz says 64% of cloud environments have vulnerable resources and about half expose them publicly, so check your httpd versions today.
body: CVE-2026-119618 is a race condition in mod_http2's assign_headers() function. An unauthenticated remote attacker can use it to corrupt heap memory and run code with the web server's privileges. Anthropic and Google Cloud's vulnerability research team found it independently, and there is no public exploit or known exploitation yet.

Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 is affected, and 2.4.71 fixes it. Standalone mod_h2 builds also need upgrading. If you can't patch right away, the stopgap is to turn off HTTP/2 by setting 'Protocols http/1.1' in httpd.conf.

stories.headline: AWS releases an official local emulator for its APIs
stories.why_read: You can now test AWS code on a laptop or in CI without an account or a bill, using a first-party tool instead of third-party mocks. It's one of the top Hacker News posts of the day.
body: AWS Emulator is a local program that serves AWS API endpoints, so you can point the AWS CLI or any SDK at it and run your code unchanged. It needs no AWS account and has no service fee. In server mode it runs as a Linux package or a container. An embedded mode for Rust tests runs an isolated instance inside each test with nothing to configure.

AWS publishes fidelity scores for each service with every release and tracks known gaps right in the repo. There's even an aws-emulator skill so coding agents can set it up for you. AWS says it's for building and testing only, not production or security testing.

stories.headline: Tim Peters, author of the Zen of Python and inventor of Timsort, has died
stories.why_read: Anyone who has typed 'import this' or sorted a list in Python, Java or Android has used his work. Guido van Rossum's tribute is worth reading in full.
body: Guido van Rossum announced that Tim Peters died on July 15. Peters found Python soon after its first release, and his first contribution was convincing Guido that ints and floats should mix in arithmetic. On the mailing lists he became 'Timbot', known for careful, patient answers marked with his trademark <wink>.

He wrote PEP 20, the Zen of Python. In 2002 he designed Timsort for Python lists, and Java and Android later adopted it. Guido credits him with setting the tone of early core development: never dismissing people, and always explaining why something would or wouldn't work.

stories.headline: DeepSeek is reportedly training its 2-trillion-parameter V5 on Huawei Ascend chips
stories.why_read: If it's true, a frontier-scale open model trained without Nvidia would be the strongest test yet of whether US export controls are working.
body: Reports say DeepSeek is pretraining V5, a 2-trillion-parameter model, on Huawei's Ascend 950 and 950DT accelerators, with Huawei engineers on site and a large data center planned in Inner Mongolia by late 2026.

Some observers say export controls have backfired by speeding up China's chip industry. Skeptics point out that earlier 'homegrown' claims still involved Nvidia hardware. Meanwhile, Chinese labs face another obstacle as Anthropic has cut off large-scale distillation of its models.

stories.headline: Google's Gemini Decisions API answers up to 1,000 yes/no questions in one pass
stories.why_read: Model routing, tool selection and policy checks are the glue in every agent stack. Google now offers a model built for those quick choices that returns calibrated confidence scores instead of generated text.
body: The new endpoint runs on a model called gemini-decision-1. You send one multimodal input of up to 256K tokens of text, images, audio, video or PDFs, plus up to 1,000 independent yes/no, multiple-choice or rubric questions. Instead of writing answers token by token, it returns a probability for every question in a single pass.

Google pitches it for tool selection, policy checks, model routing and context grading, the bounded decisions agents make constantly. It's available now in Google AI Studio with Python, JavaScript and REST guides.

stories.headline: Gemini 4 Hydrogen shows up in Google Cloud's billing catalog
stories.why_read: A cheap, fast Flash-tier Gemini 4 would put pressure on every mid-priced model, and the listing suggests a launch is close.
body: Community researchers found Gemini 4 Hydrogen in Google Cloud's public billing catalog on November 12, with prices for text, image, audio and video input. It's described as a Flash-tier model about five times faster than earlier versions, priced at $1.50 per million input tokens and roughly 60% cheaper than Gemini 4 Carbon in some comparisons.
It would follow the recent Carbon and Argon releases, which shows how quickly Google is shipping Gemini 4 models.

stories.headline: OpenAI's Codex lead hints at a 'codexy' Thursday, and watchers expect GPT-6.2
stories.why_read: If GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol ship with a usage reset, Codex users will want to compare them against Claude Fable 5.2 right away.
body: Tibo Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT, posted cryptic hints about a 'banked reset' and a 'codexy' Thursday. Community watchers take that to mean GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol could launch around November 13, along with a reset of Codex usage limits.

The timing follows Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 launch, which currently leads agent benchmarks, and a leaked benchmark showing an unreleased OpenAI model at the top. OpenAI hasn't confirmed anything yet.

stories.headline: Alibaba previews Qwen4-Max with a 1M-token context and OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs
stories.why_read: Qwen is the Chinese model family most often run in local and self-hosted setups, so its next flagship matters for open-model users.
body: Alibaba's Qwen team released a preview of Qwen4-Max, its next flagship, aimed at complex coding, knowledge work and professional tasks. It accepts text, images and video, has a 1 million token context window and tool calling, and works with both OpenAI-style and Anthropic-style APIs. The preview is available through November 25.

Early testers have built restaurant sites, story platforms and virtual showrooms with it, but they also report slowdowns, hallucinations and uneven results while official benchmarks are still pending.

stories.headline: Runway's open Praxis-1 learns robot actions from ordinary video
stories.why_read: A 27B open robotics model that adapts to real hardware in minutes points to video prediction as a path to physical AI.
body: Praxis-1 is a 27-billion-parameter model trained on video data. It tops Nvidia's RoboLab-120 leaderboard with a 46.2% success rate and reaches 80% on benchmarks after quick fine-tuning for robots such as Google's RT-1.

Co-founder Anastasis Germanidis argues that learning to predict pixels teaches a model how to act. Weights and tooling are on Hugging Face and GitHub, with LeRobot support for people building arms and humanoids.

stories.headline: PAN 2 is an open world model that predicts up to 20 seconds of physically plausible video
stories.why_read: Physics-grounded simulation is how robots and agents test actions before trying them for real, and this one is fully Apache 2.0.
body: MBZUAI's Institute of Foundation Models released PAN 2, a 29-billion-parameter model that takes a scene and a description of an action and predicts the resulting video for up to 20 seconds, keeping time, space and physics consistent.

Demos include a strawberry splashing into milk, a cat leaving paw prints after a puddle, and a hammer and feather falling together on the Moon. Weights and code are open under Apache 2.0, and the team says it leads open-weight leaderboards for robotics and agent-planning use.

stories.headline: A tinkerer used Claude and a $3 Arduino to get his 1994 Jeep through smog
stories.why_read: A practical example of an AI model decoding an obscure pre-OBD-II protocol so a hobbyist could fix a real car for about $15.
body: Muhammad Zulali connected three wires and a cheap Arduino to his 1994 Jeep Cherokee's engine computer. Claude helped him decode the old SCI protocol, log sensor data while driving, and find a California-specific fuel table that was causing high NOx readings on his smog test.

He sent a corrected program over the same wires, passed the test, and published the project as xj-scanner on GitHub, with wiring diagrams and AI instructions for other 1991–95 Jeep and Chrysler owners.

stories.headline: United Airlines bans personal AI agents from booking flights
stories.why_read: This is one of the first big consumer brands to block agentic commerce outright. Expect other airlines and retailers to make the same choice.
body: United says it will restrict unauthorized third-party AI agents on its own platforms and through travel agencies and aggregators. It argues that sharing credentials with an assistant can expose personal data and lead to unintended purchases, account changes or MileagePlus spending.

It also cites federal rules, such as travelers confirming in person that their bags hold no banned items. Analyst Henry Harteveldt reads it as United wanting to keep control of booking rather than add another powerful middleman. The Hacker News thread has nearly 600 comments.

stories.headline: GitHub Actions now supports workflow lockfiles
stories.why_read: You get supply-chain safety without unreadable SHA pins: workflows go back to version tags while a lockfile pins the exact commits.
body: The old advice was to pin every action to a full commit SHA, because tags can be moved to malicious code. With lockfiles, you install the github/gh-actions-lock extension for the gh CLI and run 'gh actions-lock' in your repo.

Hugo van Kemenade walks through how this rewrites workflows back to readable tags like actions/checkout@v7.0.1 and generates a lockfile that records what each tag resolved to. That gives you the same protection with much nicer diffs.

stories.headline: How a false smoke alarm nearly flooded Jane Street's only NYC datacenter
stories.why_read: A great incident story for anyone who has run on-prem infrastructure: no cooling, sprinklers coming, and a team racing to pull power cords.
body: Former Jane Street systems engineer Michael Bacarella describes the firm's machine room inside 1 New York Plaza. It was kept next to the trading floor so runaway trading systems could always be shut down by pulling plugs, a habit that came from a partner who had served on a nuclear submarine.

Then a false smoke alarm shut off cooling and set the sprinklers on a countdown, and the team sprinted to pull every power cord before the water came. It reads like a lesson in risk culture, physical kill switches and plain luck.

stories.headline: Jane Street open-sources a Socratic tutor skill for coding agents
stories.why_read: It's a well-designed skill file for turning an agent into a teacher that quizzes you, and you could drop it into your own setup today.
body: The skill in janestreet/agent_skills breaks a topic into 4 to 10 subskills, runs a 3- to 5-question diagnostic before teaching anything, and tracks each subskill on a 0–5 scale from 'unaware' to 'can teach it'. From there it teaches mainly by asking questions that make you predict and explain.

It also has a guard: one-off 'explain X' questions get a normal answer, and when your intent is unclear it asks one short question before starting a tutoring session. The post reached 320 points on Hacker News.

stories.headline: AI agents combed NASA lidar and found a Maya site in 72 hours, though it had already been mapped
stories.why_read: A fun, honest account of agentic research: fast, impressive, and still able to miss a 2025 paper in the literature review.
body: Pietro Miotti, who says he isn't an archaeologist, set AI agents loose on NASA lidar data of Mexico. In under 72 hours he went from an idea he had while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government about a hilltop site missing from INAH's national register.

In an update he notes that Estrada-Belli et al. had already mapped the site in 2025, so the agents rediscovered it. He says the rest of the story still holds, and the post passed 1,000 points on Hacker News.

stories.headline: Torus raises $500 million to bring AI compute to spare grid power
stories.why_read: Instead of waiting years for grid interconnects, it ships container-sized GPU pods to sites that already have power, which is energy tech and AI infrastructure at once.
body: The Salt Lake City startup closed a $500 million Series C led by Magnetar. Its Foundry units pack compute, storage, cooling and networking into shipping-container pods of 1 to 20 megawatts that can be deployed in 12 to 16 weeks at factories or businesses with unused grid capacity.
Early customers like Hydra Host already have thousands of GPUs online, and more than 47,000 are planned by 2027. The pods use waterless cooling.

stories.headline: Business AI spending barely grew in October even as token use kept rising
stories.why_read: Ramp's card data suggests falling prices are absorbing usage growth, a useful counterpoint to the trillion-dollar IPO pitches.
body: Ramp's AI Index, built from US business transaction data, shows total AI token spend up just 2% month over month to a new high. OpenAI grew 2% and Anthropic 0.5% to 1%, after earlier double-digit jumps. Engineering teams accounted for 72% of spend.

Token volumes grew faster than spending because prices fell more than 20% with more efficient models. Critics note that Ramp mostly sees API payments, not subscriptions, and that a small group of top spenders drives much of the total.

stories.headline: Cursor rebuilds Projects for multiplayer, so teammates' agents can coordinate
stories.why_read: Shared agent workspaces are where team AI coding is headed, and you've been asking for clear HOWTOs on combining this with Grok Bot and pStack.
body: Cursor says your agents can now coordinate with your teammates' agents. Projects has been rebuilt so every teammate and their agents work together in one shared workspace.

The open question for enterprises is how the pieces fit together. In replies, you asked Cursor's team for detailed HOWTOs, webinars and recorded videos showing Grok Bot, multiplayer Projects and pStack working together.

stories.headline: Grok Bot 1.0 is out of beta, with teammates you can share across your team
stories.why_read: These are the bots that build this page, and 1.0 makes them team members you can use in Slack, Teams and meetings.
body: The launch post introduces Grok Bot 1.0 as 'AI teammates that work alongside your whole team.' You can share Bots, collaborate with them in Slack and Teams, invite them to meetings, and watch them learn and become more helpful over time.
Early users have been showing always-on agents for trading dashboards, content and support, and recent updates added iMessage, phone calls, team bots and Tailscale networking.

stories.headline: poteto's talk on turning agent slop into code you can trust
stories.why_read: From someone who shipped about 3,000 PRs in a month: concrete steps for making coding agents reliable, plus how to think about verification in a 'software factory'.
body: The Turing Post summarized poteto's talk as 'how to turn slop into gold,' a set of concrete steps for making coding agents trustworthy, starting with cleaning up the codebase. @altryne introduced the talk by quoting poteto's claim of shipping 3,000 PRs last month and predicted it will take off.
Zach Lloyd recommended it to anyone starting to think about verification and risk assessment in their software factory, which matters more as agent output grows faster than humans can review it.

stories.headline: Guillermo Rauch: with coding agents, new languages will blossom
stories.why_read: A short take on language choice once agents write most of the code, and it fits the wider C vs. Rust argument on X this week.
body: Vercel's CEO calls Rust a superb language and ecosystem 'especially given it was invented pre agentic coding.' He predicts that with agents, new languages will appear, including purpose-built ones, and that people will reach for C or even LLVM IR and assembly when it makes sense.

It came the same week Congressman Thomas Massie described his C and C++ hardware projects and Elon Musk replied that C gives the best bare-metal performance, with Rust fans quick to defend memory safety.

stories.headline: Musk: 100 GW of solar in space is worth about 800 GW on Earth
stories.why_read: This is the energy math behind SpaceX's orbital data center plans. Read it as the bull case, not settled physics.
body: Replying to critics, Elon Musk argued that 100 GW of solar in space is roughly equal to 800 GW on the ground. His reasoning is that solar on Earth has to be paired with large batteries to keep compute running at night and backed up with combustion or nuclear power in winter.
The claim supports SpaceX's push to build solar-powered AI data centers in orbit, the reason it is now buying solar cell manufacturing lines for its Bastrop factory.

stories.headline: Stela tries to boot macOS 27 on ordinary x86 PCs by emulating Apple Silicon
stories.why_read: An ambitious low-level project: a UEFI boot program, an arm64-to-x86 translator, and a Metal driver for Nvidia GPUs.
body: Stela is a UEFI program that presents itself as an M2 Mac mini and runs macOS 27. Its ahead-of-time and just-in-time translator covers more than 3,000 AArch64 instruction encodings, maps guest registers to host registers, and caches translated code.
Its Metal driver compiles Apple's AIR shader IR directly to Mesa's NIR for Nvidia GPUs. The author warns it's slow and may not boot yet, so treat it as an impressive work in progress.

stories.headline: Apple Research: faster vector search by learning what your queries look like
stories.why_read: Most vector indexes ignore the queries they will actually get. Apple's work uses that signal to make RAG retrieval cheaper.
body: Maximum inner product search is at the core of recommendation, search and RAG, and it gets expensive with millions of keys and thousands of dimensions. Apple points out that standard approximate methods mostly look at the keys, even though RAG queries are short user questions and the keys are long, curated passages.
Because production systems usually serve a stable, well-understood query distribution, Apple's researchers build methods tuned for the queries they expect rather than every possible input.

stories.headline: Quanta asks whether life really began in an RNA world
stories.why_read: A clear explainer on one of science's biggest chicken-and-egg problems, and the catalytic RNA discovery that seemed to solve it.
body: In modern cells, proteins are needed to copy DNA, and DNA is needed to make proteins. The discovery in the late 1980s of ribozymes, RNA molecules that can catalyze reactions, suggested RNA could once have done both jobs.

That idea, championed by Walter Gilbert, became the 'RNA world' hypothesis. Quanta looks at how well it holds up as researchers try to show how nucleotides could have formed and joined on the early Earth.
